methodological_rigor.justification: The study integrates a large, heterogeneous resource (8,886 individuals across 29 cohorts) with a prospectively profiled discovery cohort of 14 AML patients (46 longitudinal samples) and 64 cardiogenic shock patients, and defines ESLs/DMI reproducibly with explicit preprocessing (minfi, Noob, probe filtering to 397,346 CpGs). Statistical methods are appropriate: Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, immune cell fractions and CH status; two-sided Fisher/Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction; permutation tests (1,000 iterations) for diagnosis-relapse pairing; and an explicit a priori power calculation for the cardiogenic shock sub-cohort (ssizeEpiCont, 85% power, HR 1.5). Weaknesses: dichotomization of DMI at the cohort median loses information and risks optimism; the 99.9th percentile destabilization threshold is reasonable but somewhat arbitrary; longitudinal AML series are small and selected; the proportional hazards assumption is not explicitly tested; and investigators were not blinded, as acknowledged. Overall methodology is solid with limitations transparently acknowledged.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective/prospective multi-cohort biomarker study integrating cross-sectional and longitudinal cohorts with Cox regression analyses in Framingham and a prospectively-collected cardiogenic shock cohort, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is high: DMI tracks leukemic burden longitudinally, remains informative in mutation-negative patients (potentially complementing MRD), is independently associated with CVD/CHD risk after adjustment in the Framingham Heart Study (HR 1.30 and 1.57), and provides prognostic information additive to CH mutations in cardiogenic shock (HR 3.76, p=0.006). Endpoints are patient-relevant (all-cause mortality, CVD, CHD, CHF), and the translational path to a methylation-based clinical biomarker is credible, though prospective validation and assay standardization are still required.

reporting_quality.justification: The study functions as a prognostic biomarker investigation (DMI as predictor of leukemic burden, cardiovascular risk and mortality), so REMARK is the most applicable checklist, with STROBE elements also relevant for the observational cohort analyses. Reporting is thorough: inclusion criteria, assay protocols (EZ bisulfite, EPIC array, minfi/Noob pipeline), ESL definition, destabilization threshold derivation, power calculation, covariate adjustment and multiplicity correction are explicitly stated; a sex/gender consideration section is included. Public datasets are identified with GSE accessions (GSE40279, GSE87571, GSE115278, GSE197676, GSE124413, GSE132203, GSE141682) and a Source Data file is referenced; however, no code repository (e.g., GitHub/Zenodo DOI) is cited in the preserved text, and effect-size reporting for some subgroup comparisons is limited to p-values.

novelty_literature.justification: The ESL/DMI framework is a conceptually novel inversion of standard methylation clock methodology: rather than modeling CpGs linearly associated with age, the authors anchor on a stability baseline derived from young healthy individuals and quantify deviation. This extends prior work on stochastic epimutations and DNAm outliers (e.g., Teschendorff, Gentilini) in a meaningful new direction and unifies hematological malignancy monitoring, aging biology, and cardiovascular risk under a single blood-based metric. The lineage-enriched ESL/chromatin accessibility link and the demonstration that DMI augments CH-mutation-based prognostication in cardiogenic shock are empirically new, though incremental relative to the broader epimutation literature; novelty is strong but not first-in-class.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well written, logically organized, and appropriately scoped. The abstract is quantitatively grounded (31,744 ESLs, 8,886 individuals, 29 cohorts), the Introduction builds a clear rationale from CH biology to epigenetic stability, Methods are detailed, and Results flow coherently from ESL definition to clinical correlates. Figure captions are informative and standalone-interpretable, with clear definitions of boxplot elements and statistical tests. Minor issues: some paragraphs in the Results are dense (e.g., the lineage-enriched ESL section), and the Discussion could more sharply separate biomarker claims from mechanistic speculation about TF binding.

key_strengths: Novel ESL/DMI framework unifying blood cancer monitoring, aging and cardiovascular risk under a single metric derived from 31,744 stably hypomethylated CpGs
Large, diverse evidence base (8,886 individuals, 29 cohorts) combined with prospectively profiled AML longitudinal and cardiogenic shock cohorts

Appropriate statistics with pre-specified power calculation (ssizeEpiCont, 85% power, HR 1.5), Bonferroni correction, permutation tests, and Cox models adjusted for age, sex, immune cell composition and CH status
Clinically meaningful signal: DMI independently predicts CVD/CHD in Framingham and augments CH-mutation prognostication in cardiogenic shock (HR 3.76, p=0.006)
Transparent methods with public GSE accessions and Source Data referenced, enabling partial reproducibility
key_concerns: Median-split dichotomization of DMI and a fixed 99.9th-percentile destabilization threshold risk optimistic effect sizes; sensitivity analyses with continuous DMI would strengthen inference
Longitudinal AML series are small (n=14 patients, 46 samples) and selected, limiting generalizability of the clonal-tracking claims
No explicit code-availability statement or repository DOI is preserved in the text; proportional hazards assumption is not explicitly tested
Mechanistic claims linking ESL perturbation to TF binding (e.g., KLF12/RGS2) are correlative and require functional validation
Prospective validation of DMI as a clinical biomarker (MRD complement, CVD risk stratification) is not demonstrated
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid, conceptually novel multi-cohort biomarker study with clear translational implications across hematologic malignancy monitoring and cardiovascular risk; appropriate for a strong Tier 2 venue with minor revisions addressing dichotomization sensitivity, code availability, and mechanistic caveats.
